github.title: google-research/paper-orchestra
github.abstract:
🎻 PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing Yiwen Song 1 , Yale Song 1 , Tomas Pfister 1 , and Jinsung Yoon 1 1 Google Cloud AI Research PaperOrchestra is a multi-agent framework for automated AI research paper writing. It flexibly transforms unconstrained pre-writing materials (ideas and experimental logs) into submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts, including comprehensive literature synthesis and generated visuals, such as plots and conceptual diagrams. Acting like an orchestrated team of specialized agents, it handles outline generation, literature review, section writing, content refinement, and plotting to close the gap between raw research materials and submission ready papers. Key Features Multi-Agent Pipeline : Orchestrates specialized agents (Outline, Literature Review, Section Writing, Content Refinement, Plotting) for end-to-end paper generation. Comprehensive Literature Synthesis : Automatically searches, prioritizes, and integrates relevant literature into the manuscript. Visuals Generation : Generates plots and supports the inclusion of conceptual diagrams. LaTeX Automation : Produces submission-ready LaTeX manuscripts adhering to target conference templates. Installation Environment Setup : The project relies on a Conda environment named paper_orchestra . You can set up a similar environment with Python 3.11 and install the required dependencies. conda create -n paper_orchestra python=3.11
conda activate paper_orchestra
pip install -r requirements.txt Environment Variables : Create a .env file in the root of the project and add your API keys: # Add keys if you have them, otherwise leave them empty # You need to specify related keys if you want to use the model # For example, if you want to use Gemini models, you need to specify either VERTEX_AI_PROJECT and VERTEX_AI_LOCATION, or GEMINI_API_KEY # If you want to use OpenAI models, you need to specify OPENAI_API_KEY SEMANTIC_SCHOLAR_API_KEY = your_semantic_scholar_api_key OPENAI_API_KEY = your_openai_api_key VERTEX_AI_PROJECT = your_vertex_ai_project VERTEX_AI_LOCATION = your_vertex_ai_location GEMINI_API_KEY = your_gemini_api_key # if you want to run demo and send emails to yourself at the end, set these 2 fields as well SMTP_EMAIL = your_email SMTP_PASSWORD = your_password Dataset The dataset used for paper generation is not included in this code repository. It will be released separately at a later date.
Once available, you should download the dataset and place it under the datasets/ directory. Usage You can run the paper generation pipeline using the provided bash script or directly via the Python CLI. Using the Bash Script ./paper_writing_cli.sh Using the Python CLI directly python paper_writing_cli.py \
  --raw_materials_dir /path_to_your_raw_materials/ \
  --latex_template_dir /path_to_your_latex_template/ \
  --output_dir /path_to_your_output_folder/ \
  --use_plotting true Key Arguments --raw_materials_dir : (Required) Directory containing the raw materials (e.g., idea and experimental log). --latex_template_dir : (Required) Directory containing the LaTeX template (e.g., templates/cvpr2025 ). --output_dir : Directory to output the generated paper. If not specified, an automatic folder with a timestamp is created. --use_plotting : Enable the plotting agent workflow to generate figures from code (Default: False ). --writer_model_name : LLM for writer and literature agents. --reflection_model_name : LLM for reflection agents. Interactive Demo We provide an interactive Streamlit demo for the paper generation pipeline. For instructions on how to run and use it, please refer to the README.md in the frontend directory. Project Structure autoraters/ : Contains scripts for automated evaluation. methods/ : Core logic for agents and pipeline execution. templates/ : LaTeX templates for target conferences, you can add your own template by creating a new subfolder under this directory. utils/ : Utility functions for API calls, PDF handling, etc. Citation If you find this repo or our paper helpful, please cite it as follows: @article { song2026paperorchestra , title = { PaperOrchestra: A Multi-Agent Framework for Automated AI Research Paper Writing } , author = { Song, Yiwen and Song, Yale and Pfister, Tomas and Yoon, Jinsung } , journal = { arXiv preprint arXiv:2604.05018 } , year = { 2026 } } Disclaimer This is not an officially supported Google product.

github.title: hieunc229/mailflare
github.abstract:
Mailflare A self-hosted alternative to Google Workspace. Setup custom domain Emails , Calendar, Drive, Booking and built-in AI agents . Self-host it on Cloudflare or Docker. Or try Mailflare Cloud with high-deliverable emails from $4​ Screenshots Inbox Domains Mailboxes Calendar Booking Drive Features Apps Email : Custom domain mailboxes, personal or shared, with access you control. Send and receive with Cloudflare Email, Resend or Amazon SES. Routing rules : Store, forward, reject or sort incoming mail, including a one-rule filter for newsletters and promotions. Calendar : Repeating events with time zones. Attendees get email invitations. Booking : Share a public link so anyone can book a free time on your calendar. Drive : Store and share files. AI agents : Search mail, draft replies and manage events. Connect other AI tools over MCP. Technical Databases : Cloudflare D1 (default), PostgreSQL, MySQL, Turso / libSQL, or a local SQLite file. Set DATABASE_URL to switch. Works with Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale, TiDB and more. See Databases . File storage : Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or AWS S3. Hosting : Cloudflare Workers or a single Docker container. Admin : Users, API keys, webhooks, audit logs and backups. Import : Bring in mail from IMAP, Gmail Takeout, .eml and .mbox files, and Google Calendar events, Google Contacts and Google Drive files from Takeout. See Importing from Google Takeout . Mailflare currently supports 34 languages, including English, Português (Brasil), Português (Portugal), Español, Français, Deutsch, Italiano, Nederlands, Polski, Українська, Русский, Türkçe, 中文（簡體）, 日本語, 한국어, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu, Tiếng Việt, ไทย, हिन्दी, বাংলা, मराठी, తెలుగు, தமிழ், ગુજરાતી, ಕನ್ನಡ, മലയാളം, ਪੰਜਾਬੀ, සිංහල, Kiswahili, Hausa, plus العربية, اردو and فارسی (right-to-left). Cost You can receive and send mail for free. Receiving : Cloudflare Email Routing is free. Sending : Use the free tier of Resend (3,000 emails a month) or Amazon SES. Cloudflare's own sending needs the $5/month Paid Worker plan. New Amazon SES accounts start in a sandbox. Ask AWS for production access to lift it. Prices change, so check Resend , Amazon SES and Cloudflare . Deploy Deploy the app. Click Deploy to Cloudflare . Keep the app name mailflare , or it will break. Finish setup. Open the app at /setup and create your admin account. Connect a domain. Add a domain from the same Cloudflare account, then create your first mailbox. CF_TOKEN is required. Create a scoped Cloudflare API token with these permissions: All accounts: Email Sending:Edit, DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Addresses:Edit All zones: DNS Settings:Edit, Email Routing Rules:Edit, Zone Settings:Edit, DNS:Edit More options: deployment guide . Deploy with an AI agent Paste this into an AI agent that has terminal access (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and similar): Install Mailflare for me from https://github.com/hieunc229/mailflare on my Cloudflare account.

1. Read README.md, docs/deployment.md and wrangler.jsonc first.
2. Ask me for my Cloudflare account ID and two API tokens, using a secret input:
   a deploy token (for Wrangler) and a runtime token (the Worker secret CF_TOKEN).
   Never print them, commit them, or pass them as command arguments.
3. Keep the Worker name exactly "mailflare". Create or reuse the D1 database
   "mailflare", the R2 bucket "mailflare-raw", and the queues "mailflare-inbound",
   "mailflare-outbound" and "mailflare-agent".
4. Install dependencies, run `npm run deploy`, and set CF_TOKEN as a Worker secret.
   Do not run remote database migrations yourself. The /setup page does that.
5. Give me the app URL and anything I still need to do. I will open /setup, create
   the admin account and connect my domain. Token permissions and more options: deployment guide . Self-host with Docker Runs as one container on any server, with SQLite and local files. cp .env.docker.example .env.docker
docker compose up -d --build Or skip the build and run the prebuilt image: docker compose -f docker-compose.image.yml up -d . See self-hosting . Local development cp .dev.vars.example .dev.vars
npm install
npm run db:migrate:local
npm run dev Add your Cloudflare credentials to .dev.vars , then open localhost:3000 . Run npm run db:seed to load sample data. npm run build : build the Worker npm run deploy : build and deploy npm run lint : lint and type check A schema change needs a migration for each database type. See Databases . Documentation Deployment and configuration Databases Sending and receiving providers API and integrations Email assistant and MCP Importing from Google Takeout Adding a language Troubleshooting License See LICENSE .

github.title: superdesigndev/treg
github.abstract:
Treg (OpenRouter for Tools) OpenRouter, but for agent tools instead of models. Point an agent at one base URL with one token
and it can do the job: a curated catalog of thousands of endpoints across many providers — SEO and backlinks,
social and trends, people and company enrichment, ads, scraping, image and video generation — priced per call, from a cent ,
with no provider signup. Plus your own team's keys, skills and CLIs, callable by every teammate's
agent without the credential ever leaving the server. Ask for the task, not the tool. You do not need to know which vendor sells backlink data, or to
hold an account with them. Search for what you want to do, read the price, call it. Built for the Superdesign team, live at treg.to — anyone can self-host. Why it exists The tools an agent needs for real work sit behind subscriptions nobody buys for a single run —
Semrush $139/mo, Moz $99/mo, Crunchbase $99/mo, Apollo $59/seat — behind signup walls, or behind no
public API at all (invite-only, partner-only, app-review-only). treg carries those accounts and
bills fractions of a cent per call. Two kinds of tool, one token The catalog — external endpoints treg can serve with its own key or through a verified public
route that needs no provider key. Own-key calls use the team's prepaid balance; anonymous calls
are free. No account with the provider is needed. New verified accounts receive $1.00 free once, when they create an eligible team. Your own tools — anything a teammate registered: a paid API account, an OAuth connection, a
vendor CLI, a SKILL.md . Your own key always wins over treg's, and those calls are never
metered. The vocabulary for the second half: tool = something the registry calls for you with the org's credential. Two kinds: endpoint — an upstream base_url + credential bindings (each binding injects one
secret into the request; a request can carry several, e.g. an OAuth bearer and a developer-token header). CLI — a vendor binary ( stripe , gh , vercel , ...) run with the credential injected. skill / bundle = a recipe ( SKILL.md ) + its secrets + its tool(s), registered together. The one rule: the proxy relays, never models the upstream, and injects auth server-side — so it survives upstream API changes and callers never hold keys. Part 1 · Using the registry Visit treg.to (hosted on Render) — the dashboard,
sign-in, and every URL below live there. Quickstart Same flow as the dashboard's Getting started guide: # 1. install the CLI — also points it at the registry curl -fsSL https://treg.to/install.sh | sh # 2. sign in (GitHub default · --email for a one-time code · --token for agents/CI) treg login # 3. do something useful immediately — no key, nothing registered treg catalog search " backlinks for a domain " # find a tool by what it DOES treg call tikhub.tiktok.user.profile --query uniqueId=tiktok
treg balance # exactly what that cost # (or `treg onboard` for the guided walkthrough) Fish Audio provides S2.1 Pro speech, public-voice discovery, and private voice cloning.
Speech is binary stdout, so redirect it to a file. A discovered voice's _id or a team voice id is
the TTS reference_id ; voices created on treg's Fish account are durable team resources: treg call fishaudio.tts.s2-1-pro --method POST --header model=s2.1-pro \
  --data ' {"text":"Hello from treg","format":"mp3"} ' > speech.mp3
treg call fishaudio.voices.discover --query self=false --query licensed=false --query language=en
treg resources list --provider fishaudio --kind voice With your own Fish key, requests are an unmetered upstream relay and Fish owns the account boundary. A client written for a provider's own API can switch by its base URL alone: https://treg.to/call/<provider> in place of the provider's base URL ( https://api.dataforseo.com/v3 → https://treg.to/call/dataforseo ) runs the catalog tool on that method and path exactly as /call/<id> would; a path the catalog does not list is a 404, never relayed. Catalog tool inputs are described by treg catalog get <id> . Tools marked strict_query reject undeclared or repeated query parameters, unsupported values and request bodies. Send each declared parameter within its declared type, allowed values and range, each single-valued one once, and a row count such as limit as a whole number within its stated maximum: a tool that enforces this answers a 400 catalog_parameter_invalid naming the parameter, and nothing is charged. Undeclared fields are forwarded as sent. Your token identifies you on every call ( X-Treg-Token header) and is the same for all tools.
Discover what your team has shared: treg tool ls · check credential health: treg health . Or install it as a Claude Code plugin /plugin marketplace add superdesigndev/treg
/plugin install treg@treg Installs the treg skill and treg's tools with no token and no configuration. Run /mcp , pick
treg and sign in; the tools appear after it. Other agents: npx skills add superdesigndev/treg -s treg (or see Workflow skills for the rest).
See docs/CLAUDE-PLUGIN.md . MiniMax Code / MiniMax Agent users: the same
skill ships via the MiniMax Plugin Marketplace ( docs/MINIMAX-PLUGIN.md ). Workflow skills Ready-made recipes your agent runs end to end, every call through treg: Skill What your agent can do treg Find and call any tool in the catalog, plus your own tools web-access When your agent's own web tools fall short, read the live web without local scrapers: free search and page reads first, then the right platform job for social, stores, reviews, maps and papers, with treg falling back to the next vendor when one fails lead-signals Find in-market buyers from public signals (complaints, job changes, hiring, funding, tool adoption) and monitor a topic, competitor or account list for them ( treg.to/leads-signals ) recruit Turn a LinkedIn job post into a ranked shortlist: criteria from the post, people search, filters with reasons, one line on why each fits, cited evidence (posts, GitHub, talks, tenure, job change) under a per-candidate spend cap, then a checked personal email and phone, with a run file of counts, evidence and the vendor trail per candidate doomscroll Catch up on any topic over the last hours: the best posts, clips and reactions from X, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Hacker News and Product Hunt, grouped into stories with links, only what is new since the last scroll make-ugc Make AI UGC videos: trending hooks, a presenter, talking-head clips, captions ( treg.to/ugc ) jev-memory Give Claude Code a memory: a Claude Code mod where Jev judges each prompt after the turn and keeps your lasting preferences, installed ready-made or built from one prompt ( the mod ) install.sh installs only treg and names the others in one line; your agent offers them after
sign-in and the first call. Name the ones you want with sh -s -- --skills lead-signals,recruit (or --skills all ; the opt-in jev-memory and rea-growth are never in that set). In Claude Code each one is
also its own plugin in treg's marketplace: /plugin install recruit@treg , or pick them from /plugin . To add
them to an existing agent instead ( skills.sh CLI): npx skills add superdesigndev/treg # every public skill npx skills add superdesigndev/treg --skill lead-signals # just one treg skill bootstrap --skills all # the installer's set, with the treg CLI you already have The workflow skills run on treg, so set it up first (the Quickstart above, or point your agent at treg.to/llms.txt ). Claude.ai connector The Claude Connectors Directory surface is https://treg.to/mcp/v2/ . It exposes only curated
catalog endpoints, without image, video or audio generation, and separates read calls from write
calls so Claude receives accurate safety signals. The existing /mcp/ surface remains available for catalog endpoints, team-owned tools,
and imported skills. See the MCP and OAuth architecture for the boundary and implementation, and the submission runbook for release gates.

others.title: From words to work: how AI social language boosts productivity and creative self-efficacy
others.abstract:
While AI agents enhance productivity, they may also threaten human autonomy and creativity in collaborative tasks. Balancing efficiency with individual capability development is key to advancing human–AI collaboration.
 
 
 
 Based on Emotions as Social Information theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this research conducted two studies to explore how AI social-oriented language influences perceived collaboration outcomes, specifically perceived work productivity and creative self-efficacy. Study 1 employed a questionnaire survey in general work and life collaboration contexts. Study 2 employed a simulated interaction experiment involving specific tasks.
 
 
 
 Study 1 demonstrated the positive effects of AI social-oriented language on both perceived work productivity and creative self-efficacy, with perceived AI-supported autonomy mediating these effects. Study 2 further supported these relationships and revealed the boundary conditions of task type. Specifically, for creative tasks, highly social-oriented AI language enhanced both perceived AI-supported autonomy and collaboration outcomes, whereas for routine analytical tasks, these effects were not significant.
 
 
 
 This study not only addresses current concerns regarding collaboration performance but also highlights the human-centered value of AI by emphasizing creative potential. It bridges the gap by linking AI language style to these concrete outcomes. The findings enrich the understanding of AI language design in human–AI collaboration and provide both theoretical and practical implications for optimizing AI interaction strategies to improve collaboration outcomes.

others.title: S³: A Multicriteria Pre-Deployment Scoring Protocol for Enterprise Small Language Model Selection
others.abstract: Technology managers lack a systematic protocol for determining which enterprise workloads are safe for local small language model deployment. We introduce S³ (Suitability Score for SLM Selection), a multicriteria framework that scores workloads across six dimensions, Task Complexity, Output Structure, Stakeholder Risk, Data Sensitivity, Latency Tolerance, and Volume Load, and assigns them to Pure SLM, Hybrid, or LLM-Only tiers before inference. Non-compensatory gate rules enforce safety constraints for high-stakes scenarios, ensuring that life-critical or expert-level generative tasks are never assigned to a local model regardless of their aggregate score. Thresholds calibrated on an independent use-case set correctly predicted all eight held-out tier assignments across six industries, with Pure SLM tiers achieving at least 95% LLM parity.

others.title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
others.abstract: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

others.title: Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
others.abstract: Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8x and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

others.title: Modern Self-Supervised Vision Transformers Are Pareidolic
others.abstract: In human perception, pareidolia is the tendency to perceive a meaningful pattern, such as a face, in a random or ambiguous stimulus.We find a similar phenomenon in modern self-supervised Vision Transformers (ViTs): on white noise, which contains neither objects nor spatial structure, a few directions of their features still form spatially coherent patterns across the patches, imposed by the features themselves.We call this behavior pareidolia, and the span of these directions the pareidolic subspace.On natural images, it holds most of the feature variance in DINOv2 and DINOv3 but little in DINO.This excess explains why DINOv2 and DINOv3, despite stronger dense features, fall far behind DINO in object emergence, the hallmark ability of self-supervised ViTs to identify the patches of an object on their own.Our experiments further show that scaling down their pareidolic subspaces steadily restores their ability to discover objects, so their object emergence is hindered rather than lost.These findings naturally lead to a training-free calibration: Pareidolia Subspace Calibration(PSC) measures the pareidolic subspace only on a noise input and then calibrates the features of natural inputs by scaling its directions down to the variance level of the remaining directions.Across diverse object emergence tasks, PSC improves DINOv2 and DINOv3 by up to 31.7 CorLoc on object discovery, 30.2 maxF on saliency detection and 59.9~$\mathcal{J}$ on video object segmentation.To identify the cause of pareidolia, we trace it block by block and find that it forms in the middle blocks of every self-supervised model we examine but stays strong to the last block only in models trained with a patch-level loss; controlled training confirms that an image-level loss alone lets it fade.

others.title: Let Vision-Language Models Generate Images through Their Representations
others.abstract: Recent unified multimodal models aim to combine visual understanding and generation within a single model, yet effectively integrating the two capabilities remains challenging. Leveraging pretrained vision-language models offers a way to build on already learned multimodal knowledge, but making this knowledge effectively accessible to visual generation remains nontrivial. We find that a central challenge lies in the heterogeneous visual representations used for understanding and generation. To address this challenge, we introduce Integral, which converts a pretrained vision-language model into a unified multimodal model by constructing a shared visual representation space across the two capabilities. Integral implements this design through two complementary components. Abstraction Fusion constructs shared visual tokens by aggregating hierarchical representations from the frozen vision encoder, while Block-wise MoT introduces a lightweight generative stream that interacts with the vision-language model only at block boundaries. Our approach effectively preserves the pretrained understanding capability while extending it to strong visual generation. Controlled comparisons further demonstrate that sharing visual representations between understanding and generation substantially improves generative learning compared with using a separate visual representation space, despite comparable reconstruction fidelity. These results suggest that representations learned by pretrained vision-language models already provide an effective foundation for visual generation.

others.title: TowerBridge: Bridging the Dual-Encoder Modality Gap via Weight-Space Programming
others.abstract: CLIP-style dual encoders map images and text through two separate towers into a shared embedding space, where the two modalities occupy distinct regions separated by a modality gap. Retrieval fails when wrong matches, or hard negatives, outrank the correct one, and the gap is the usual suspect. Yet removing it post hoc degrades retrieval on every CLIP checkpoint we test. We introduce a paired statistic that identifies directions where the two towers agree more on hard negatives than on matched pairs. Mildly attenuating these directions improves retrieval while largely preserving the gap. We arrive at this correction through weight-space programming: guided by the statistic, an LLM agent inspects both towers and writes closed-form weight edits without backpropagation. Free to edit any component, the agent improves COCO test retrieval on all 13 CLIP checkpoints and edits an output projection in 12 of the 13. We distill and refine its recurring correction into TowerBridge, a closed-form recipe motivated by a first-order analysis of the hard-negative margin. Computed in seconds from 25,000 labelled pairs, it requires no model-specific tuning and leaves the architecture and inference cost unchanged. TowerBridge improves COCO test retrieval by 16.8 RSUM and Flickr30k test retrieval by 6.6 on average across all 21 evaluated CLIP checkpoints, including 8 unseen by the agent, while limiting any drop in ImageNet zero-shot accuracy to 0.5 points. It also reduces hubness on all 21 checkpoints and improves retrieval on 4 of 5 dual encoders from other families.

others.title: Language Models Steer on Injected Uncertainty Tokens, but Fail to Self-Monitor In Situ
others.abstract:
Prompting language models to verbalize stepwise numerical confidence during generation is an increasingly popular approach for triggering backtracking and error correction in agentic reasoning. This strategy presupposes two capabilities: (1) in-situ monitoring fidelity (does confidence drop when an error occurs?) and (2) downstream steering control (does an uncertainty token causally steer the model to repair its error?). We evaluated four open-weights models (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4, 14.7B) across 15,200 math benchmark attempts, isolating 2,017 reasoning errors within each model's capability frontier. Applying 27,568 counterfactual continuations across these failure points, we demonstrate a consistent decoupling between monitoring and control.
  On monitoring, all four models fail to detect their own errors. Verbalized confidence does not distinguish mistake steps from sound reasoning, yielding near-chance within-position AUROCs between 0.500 and 0.561. Even at a model's first reasoning error, trajectory confidence remains saturated at 95.1% to 99.9%, with noticeable drops ($\ge 10$ points) appearing on fewer than 9% of errors in Llama and under 1.6% in the other three models. In contrast, models respond readily to external uncertainty: injecting a low-confidence tag (10%) at the error step significantly increases downstream correction across all models (+3.7 to +22.5 points over format-matched 95% certainty; all $p \le 0.0022$), reaching up to 38.5% under active rethinking instructions. However, injecting doubt onto already-correct steps causes models to discard valid reasoning, reducing solve rates by up to 22.8 points. Inference-time self-correction is thus bottlenecked by in-situ error detection rather than downstream repair capacity: models readily steer toward recovery when prompted with doubt, yet fail to self-monitor during generation.

others.title: How Far Can Linear Go? BiPert, a Unified Framework for Single-Cell Perturbation Modelling
others.abstract: Understanding how genetic perturbations affect cellular behaviour is essential for studying gene function and regulatory mechanisms. Large-scale CRISPR screens measure these effects across thousands of genes, but cover relatively few cellular contexts. Predicting perturbation responses in unseen cell types and identifying perturbed genes from their transcriptional effects therefore remain challenging. Here, we show that both tasks can be addressed through a common linear decomposition of transcriptional responses into shared and perturbation-specific components. Building on this principle, we introduce BiPert, a simple linear framework for both forward perturbation prediction and inverse identification. For forward prediction, BiPert outperforms existing methods that use no external biological knowledge when predicting gene expression changes in unseen cell lines. Its few-shot extension, BiPert-FS, adapts to new cell lines using as few as ten measured perturbations. For inverse identification, BiPert-ID identifies perturbed genes from single-cell expression profiles, outperforming deep-learning methods in unseen cell lines and donors. We further show that perturbations whose effects transfer more consistently across cellular contexts are also easier to identify, even after controlling for perturbation effect size. Together, these results establish a connection between perturbation transfer and identification, and demonstrate that simple linear models provide strong, interpretable baselines for both tasks.

others.title: Self-Supervised Dataset Distillation via Mutual Information Maximization
others.abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) aims to compress a large dataset into a small synthetic one that remains effective for training neural networks. Despite its success in supervised learning, DD remains underexplored in self-supervised learning (SSL), where distilled data must preserve the information needed to learn representations that remain consistent across augmentations. To bridge this gap, we introduce Mutual Information Prototype Alignment (MIPA), an efficient SSL dataset distillation approach that optimizes synthetic images to preserve augmentation-invariant information. Specifically, MIPA treats synthetic images as learnable prototypes and uses a frozen encoder to assign real samples to them based on feature similarity. A synthetic dataset that preserves such augmentation invariance should yield stable prototype assignments across multiple augmented views of the same real image. MIPA encourages this by maximizing mutual information between cross-view assignments while avoiding trivial solutions in which all real samples are assigned to only a few synthetic prototypes. Evaluations on image classification benchmarks show that synthetic data generated by MIPA yield higher-quality representations than existing distillation approaches while reducing time and storage demands during distillation.

others.title: Agentic AI for Intent Management and Control in Autonomous Communication Networks
others.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation will help future mobile networks translate high-level network intents into concrete network optimization or control actions. However, existing approaches often focus on intent management and orchestration, leaving the adaptation of underlying network optimization and control functions largely unaddressed. This article proposes a triadic agentic AI framework that co-designs intent management and intent fulfillment through three agents: an interpreter, powered by a language model, that translates and refines intents into machine-readable optimization templates; an optimizer that adapts controller policies to intent specifications; and a controller that performs fast decision-making. We discuss the design space of each agent and how the workflow can be embedded across network architectural domains. Finally, we develop a concrete realization combining a language-model interpreter with Bayesian optimization for the optimizer and multi-objective reinforcement learning for the controller, and evaluate it in a radio resource management case study for differentiated connectivity. Results demonstrate how the agentic AI framework can connect high-level intents with runtime network control, showing adaptability of intent specifications and control policies to service requirements and changing network conditions.

others.title: CTLink: A Text-Prompted Segmentation Model for Linking Radiology Report Findings to 3D Chest CT Scans
others.abstract: Radiology reports describe findings in text only, without visually marking them on the scan, so readers cannot directly see which abnormality each reported finding refers to. We introduce CTLink, a text-prompted 3D segmentation model that segments findings described in a chest CT report. CTLink was trained on 4123 noncontrast chest CT scans with 9547 segmented report findings, including ReXGroundingCTv2, a newly annotated dataset of 1134 scans and 1895 findings with every instance of each finding segmented. On the 200 ReXGroundingCT validation scans, CTLink achieved a hit rate of 0.816, an instance F1 score of 0.456, and a mean Dice score of 0.400, compared with 0.533, 0.175, and 0.234 for VoxTell, a publicly available text-prompted segmentation model (P < .001 for all). On the test set of the MICCAI 2026 ReXGrounding challenge, an ensemble of seven CTLink models achieved the highest hit rate (0.782) and instance F1 score (0.386) of all 48 participating teams. On 50 test scans segmented twice by independent radiologists, CTLink matched or exceeded inter-rater agreement. Diffuse non-focal findings remained the main limitation, partly because their extent is outlined inconsistently even between radiologists. The CTLink model weights are available at https://huggingface.co/rajpurkarlab/CTLink, and the dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/rajpurkarlab/ReXGroundingCT.

others.title: LeJEPA Features Are Not Isotropic, and Should Not Be
others.abstract: The SIGReg term in LeJEPA regularizes features to have an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Our first result is to show that this regularizer, in practice, cannot achieve its goal. We design a modified regularizer to enforce the objective better. This leads to slightly improved performance. For example, on ImageNet-100, our modified regularizer reaches the final accuracy of SIGReg in 1.3$\times$ fewer epochs. Our second result argues that self-supervised encoders should not have isotropic Gaussian features. We show that the alignment term in LeJEPA conflicts with SIGReg, because it couples the magnitude of the features with their directions. In contrast, isotropic Gaussian features would entail independent magnitude and directions. Features obtained with LeJEPA are, in fact, not isotropic. So LeJEPA has two issues. Its regularizer is weak, and the isotropic Gaussian target is too strict. Our third result is about reformulating the isotropic Gaussian regularizer to enforce only the marginal distributions of the magnitude and direction, without enforcing independence. This leads to a simple regularization term, PolarReg, that can be optimized reliably across many different datasets, batch sizes and embedding dimensions without any hyper-parameter changes. On ImageNet-1k, our technique matches the accuracy of LeJEPA and its variants in 4.7$\times$ fewer epochs. It improves the final accuracy by 1.8 points.

others.title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
others.abstract: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.

others.title: Flood forecasting using a physics-guided conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model
others.abstract: High-resolution flood forecasting with full two-dimensional shallow water equation (SWE) solvers remains computationally expensive, even on GPUs. We develop a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) that forecasts the evolution of 30 m water-depth fields over a four-day horizon for the Des Plaines River watershed, Illinois. The model is trained on SynxFlow SWE simulations of 113 historical storms observed across twelve Midwestern states (2003-2024), each under three antecedent-wetness scenarios, and can optionally be conditioned on coarse 100 m or 150 m hydrodynamic simulations. Because reverse diffusion is stochastic, every forecast is a 20-member ensemble drawn from the same trained model. Coarse conditioning reduces the four-day mean water-depth RMSE of the ensemble mean from 0.170 m to 0.054 m (100 m) and 0.048 m (150 m). The coarser 150 m conditioning also gives the best critical success index (0.839), false alarm ratio, CRPS and Brier score at lower cost, so finer conditioning does not guarantee better skill. Averaging members reduces error by 5-11% relative to a single realization, and the ensemble provides spatially explicit exceedance probabilities, although the ensembles are under-dispersive (spread-to-error ratios 0.35-0.73). On a single GPU, a four-day forecast over 26 non-overlapping patches is 7.8x, 11.0x and 16.3x faster than the 30 m simulation for the 100 m, 150 m and unconditioned configurations, and projected speedups for a 14-day forecast reach 12-49x for one member and 48-58x for 20 members. Physics-guided diffusion models are thus promising probabilistic surrogates for regional-scale flood forecasting.

others.title: Verifying the Outputs of PDE Solvers: From Finite Elements to Neural Surrogates
others.abstract: Physics simulation outputs increasingly come from solvers that no expert inspects, such as third-party packages in automated pipelines, programs written by large language models (LLMs), and learned surrogates. In earlier work on cardiac pulsed field ablation, we proposed that solvers return a certificate with their answers. The certificate consists of an admissible potential and an exactly charge-conserving current, and a small independent checker turns it into guaranteed error bounds against a written specification of the physics. Here, the same checker verifies the outputs of other solvers on the same problem. Specifically, FEniCSx computes both fields and receives the same bounds as our own solver. Five plausible bugs in a correct solver, one of them about 0.2% from the true impedance, all converge and pass a grid convergence study, yet the certificate rejects or refutes all five. Of three solvers written by LLMs, one is correct and certified to 0.1%, and one never solves the equation but converges. Neural networks that predict the coefficients of a reduced basis emit admissible fields and receive valid per-prediction bounds, at most 0.0021% wide inside their training range and 0.3-25% wide outside it, where 90% conformal intervals cover none of 14 tests. Untuned Fourier neural operators with free nodal outputs receive valid but uninformative bounds. On a uniform grid, interpolation onto the certificate grid limits them, and on the certificate grid, thin cells turn small nodal errors into large energy errors. Energy-norm training narrows the certified interval tenfold, and projecting the nodal-loss outputs onto the reduced basis narrows it by two to four orders of magnitude, still uninformative. The guarantee concerns the stated model and holds for any output, wherever its input lies. It is informative only when the output is accurate in energy on a grid that resolves the problem.

others.title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
others.abstract: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

others.title: Matching Under Metric Privacy
others.abstract: We study how to represent and randomize points in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space to obtain accurate bipartite matchings under metric privacy. Given $n$ private and $n$ public points, we analyze local mechanisms that randomize each private point or its distances to the public points. Using the public points' affine span, we construct a smaller representation that preserves all matching costs. When a trusted server receives the private points, we establish privacy and utility guarantees for Gumbel matching, which randomizes edge costs and releases only the assignment. Through upper bounds and worst-case constructions, we establish the tight rate $Θ\!\left(n\min\{d,\log n\}/\varepsilon\right)$ for expected cost above the nonprivate optimum. Benchmark experiments support $d\approx\log n$ as a practical guide to the transition between directly randomizing point coordinates and using Gumbel matching. Extensions to squared Euclidean costs enable private nonparametric two-sample hypothesis testing. These results show how the application's trust model guides representation and dimension choices for better utility: under local privacy, low-dimensional point representations reduce excess cost, while under central privacy, distance representations achieve the optimal rate even in high dimension.
